message.content: Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). - security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: I'll start by reading redu.md to understand the deployment context.

content.content:
1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/umami-software/umami
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest
7	  port: 3000
8	  vm: m1.medium
9	  flavor_id: "3"
10	  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: umami
16	quirks:
17	  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Umami publishes a prebuilt image and the Postgres build has its own tag: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest. There is a ghcr.io/umami-software/umami mirror; the docs name the docker.umami.is one, so prefer it. Pin a version tag rather than a floating -latest once you know which one you ran, so a redeploy cannot silently jump a major version."
18	  - "⛔ THE LOGIN IS PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. A fresh Umami seeds one account, username admin, and the first-login value for it is written in Umami's own public install docs. The URL is reachable from the moment the container is healthy, so between boot and the first password change ANYONE who knows the product can sign in. This is worse than an unclaimed first-run wizard: there is no window where the instance is unowned and inert. Change it the moment the deploy reports ready, before doing anything else, and hand the new value to the user in the session."
19	  - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET EXPLICITLY. It signs the session cookies. Left unset, Umami derives one from the database connection string, so the day anything about that string changes (a rotated database password, a rebuilt managed DB, a move between environments) every existing session is invalidated and every logged-in user is silently signed out. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and keep passing the SAME one on every redeploy."
20	  - "DATABASE: Umami reads DATABASE_URL natively, and deploy_compose with database:'managed' APPENDS DATABASE_URL to the project .env already. This is the easy one: unlike n8n there is no remapping to do. Your compose still has to reference it explicitly (DATABASE_URL: \"\${DATABASE_URL}\"), because deploy_compose writes the .env and never edits your compose file. Managed-DB defaults are database `app` and user `appuser`, which is fine; Umami creates its own tables inside whatever database it is given."
21	  - "⛔ DO NOT ADD CLICKHOUSE. The redu MCP has a standing rule that analytics apps which store every event (Plausible, PostHog, Matomo, SigNoz) need a SECOND datastore and tells you to pass needs_clickhouse:true. Umami on the postgresql image does NOT: it stores events in the same Postgres. There is a separate ClickHouse build of Umami, and this is not it. Following the general rule here provisions a whole managed ClickHouse the app never connects to, and quietly doubles the bill."
22	  - "PORT 3000. The container listens there and the healthcheck Umami ships hits http://localhost:3000/api/heartbeat, which is also the cheapest thing to curl from the VM to prove the app is really up rather than merely running."
23	  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. Umami runs its own Prisma migrations at container start. On a fresh managed Postgres the first boot takes noticeably longer than later ones while it creates the schema; that is not a hang."
24	  - "TRACKING SCRIPT: the snippet Umami hands you points at /script.js on the instance's own hostname, so it works on the *.redu.cloud URL with no extra wiring. If the user later moves it to their own domain, the snippet they already pasted into their site keeps pointing at the old host."
25	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill), port 3000."
26	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Passing the Umami GitHub URL would make redu try to build the app instead of pulling the published image."
27	  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin password you set and the APP_SECRET you generate are the user's, not yours to publish. Hand both over in the session and tell them to store them. The deploy log records THAT the account was secured, never what it was secured with."
28	  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. The next person's deploy starts from yours."
29	  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but deliberately keeps the managed Postgres so analytics history is not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."
30	---
31	
32	# Self-host Umami on redu
33	
34	Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
35	URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.
36	
37	## What this deploys
38	
39	- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
40	- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
41	- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
42	
43	About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.
44	
45	## Deploy
46	
47	Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
48	directory containing this file:
49	
50	    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.
51	
52	The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.
53	
54	## The two that actually break it
55	
56	**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
57	Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
58	Change it immediately, not later.
59	
60	**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
61	signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
62	logged out.
63	
64	## Securing the admin account
65	
66	Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else.
67	
68	```bash
69	#!/usr/bin/env bash
70	# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
71	#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
72	set -eu
73	HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"
74	
75	TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
76	
77	# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
78	NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"
79	
80	# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
81	# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
82	CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"
83	
84	api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }
85	
86	# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
87	code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
88	  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
89	[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
90	TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
91	USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
92	[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }
93	
94	# 2. rotate it.
95	code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
96	  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/users/$USERID/password" \
97	        -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
98	[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "password change failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
99	
100	# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
101	code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
102	  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
103	[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }
104	
105	# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
106	code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
107	  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
108	[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }
109	
110	cat <<EOF
111	
112	Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
113	  URL:      https://$HOST
114	  Username: admin
115	  New:      $NEW
116	
117	Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
118	EOF
119	```
120	
121	It prints the new value once. It does not go in this file.
122	
123	## Deploy log
124	
125	- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and
126	  hourly rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong.

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it.
code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/users/$USERID/password" \
        -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "password change failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Username: admin
  New:      $NEW

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
EOF
```

It prints the new value once. It does not go in this file.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it.
code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/users/$USERID/password" \
        -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "password change failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Username: admin
  New:      $NEW

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
EOF

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it.
code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/users/$USERID/password" \
        -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "password change failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Username: admin
  New:      $NEW

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it.
code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/users/$USERID/password" \
        -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "password change failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Username: admin
  New:      $NEW

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
EOF
```

It prints the new value once. It does not go in this file.

done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "password change failed on every known route" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it. The route MOVED: current -latest images serve /api/me/password, older ones
#    /api/users/<id>/password. Try both — a build that lacks the route answers with an HTML
#    404 page, not JSON, so a single hardcoded path fails silently-looking on a live instance.
rotated=""
for path in "/api/me/password" "/api/users/$USERID/password"; do
  code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
    | api -X POST "https://$HOST$path" \
          -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then rotated="$path"; break; fi
  echo "  $path -> HTTP $code" >&2
done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "password change failed on every known route" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Username: admin
  New:      $NEW

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
EOF
```

It prints the new value once. It does not go in this file.

- Not yet deployed. The first real run replaces this line with its measured time, flavor and
  hourly rate, and corrects anything above that turned out to be wrong.

Umami creates its own tables inside whatever database it is given, so the names do not matter — note the DB is named after the DEPLOYMENT, not `app`: deploy #419 with name:'umami' produced database `umami` on VM `db-umami` (pass db_name/db_user to override)."
  - "⛔ DO NOT ADD CLICKHOUSE. The redu MCP has a standing rule that analytics apps which store every event (Plausible, PostHog, Matomo, SigNoz) need a SECOND datastore and tells you to pass needs_clickhouse:true. Umami on the postgresql image does NOT: it stores events in the same Postgres. There is a separate ClickHouse build of Umami, and this is not it. Following the general rule here provisions a whole managed ClickHouse the app never connects to, and quietly doubles the bill."
  - "PORT 3000. The container listens there and the healthcheck Umami ships hits http://localhost:3000/api/heartbeat, which is also the cheapest thing to curl from the VM to prove the app is really up rather than merely running."
  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. Umami runs its own Prisma migrations at container start. On a fresh managed Postgres the first boot takes noticeably longer than later ones while it creates the schema; that is not a hang."
  - "TRACKING SCRIPT: the snippet Umami hands you points at /script.js on the instance's own hostname, so it works on the *.redu.cloud URL with no extra wiring. If the user later moves it to their own domain, the snippet they already pasted into their site keeps pointing at the old host."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill), port 3000."
  - "PLAN_DEPLOY WILL SIZE THIS AT m1.large — OVERRIDE IT. needs_compose:true raises the app VM to a build-capable floor (m1.large, GBP 0.0486/hr) because it assumes a compose stack builds something. This one builds NOTHING; it pulls a published image. Left alone the plan quotes GBP 0.066/hr against a real GBP 0.0452/hr, so pass flavor_id '3' to deploy_compose explicitly. plan_deploy raises this itself as the `flavor-differs-from-record` preflight once this file records m1.medium — answer it by keeping m1.medium. Measured on m1.medium: pull + first boot + Prisma migrations on an empty DB completed in about 5.5 minutes total, so the small VM is not the bottleneck."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Passing the Umami GitHub URL would make redu try to build the app instead of pulling the published image."
  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin password you set and the APP_SECRET you generate are the user's, not yours to publish. Hand both over in the session and tell them to store them. The deploy log records THAT the account was secured, never what it was secured with."
  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. The next person's deploy starts from yours."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but deliberately keeps the managed Postgres so analytics history is not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else. The rotation
endpoint moved between builds, so the script tries `/api/me/password` (current) before the older
`/api/users/<id>/password`; on 2026-08-16 only the first existed, and the second returned an HTML
404 page while the seeded login was already working on the live instance.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it. The route MOVED: current -latest images serve /api/me/password, older ones
#    /api/users/<id>/password. Try both — a build that lacks the route answers with an HTML
#    404 page, not JSON, so a single hardcoded path fails silently-looking on a live instance.
rotated=""
for path in "/api/me/password" "/api/users/$USERID/password"; do
  code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
    | api -X POST "https://$HOST$path" \
          -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then rotated="$path"; break; fi
  echo "  $path -> HTTP $code" >&2
done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "password change failed on every known route" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Username: admin
  New:      $NEW

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
EOF
```

It prints the new value once. It does not go in this file.

last_deploy:
  id: 419
  date: 2026-08-16
  status: ready
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/umami-software/umami
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest
  port: 3000
  vm: m1.medium
  flavor_id: "3"
  database: managed postgres (redu-managed, own private VM, m1.small via db_flavor_id "2")
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0452
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp

quirks:
  - "DO NOT BUILD FROM SOURCE. Umami publishes a prebuilt image and the Postgres build has its own tag: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest. There is a ghcr.io/umami-software/umami mirror; the docs name the docker.umami.is one, so prefer it (docker.umami.is is a proxy in front of ghcr.io — a 401 on the registry API sends you to realm https://ghcr.io/token, and an anonymous pull token from there works)."
  - "⛔ YOU CANNOT PIN THIS BY VERSION TAG. Measured 2026-08-16: postgresql-latest resolved to sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:69c7fc1c», built 2026-08-12, and its digest matches NO published version tag. The newest tagged builds are far older — postgresql-v2.20.2 (2025-12-12) and postgresql-3.0.0 (2025-11-07) — so -latest is a rolling build months ahead of the tag list, and 'pin the version tag you ran' is not achievable: there isn't one. Pin the DIGEST instead: docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:69c7fc1c». Re-resolve it before each deploy with a HEAD on /v2/umami-software/umami/manifests/postgresql-latest and read docker-content-digest — and keep the Accept header IDENTICAL between calls, because a different Accept returns a different manifest and therefore a different digest, which will look like a version change when nothing moved."
  - "⛔ THE LOGIN IS PUBLICLY DOCUMENTED. A fresh Umami seeds one account, username admin, and the first-login value for it is written in Umami's own public install docs. The URL is reachable from the moment the container is healthy, so between boot and the first password change ANYONE who knows the product can sign in. This is worse than an unclaimed first-run wizard: there is no window where the instance is unowned and inert. Change it the moment the deploy reports ready, before doing anything else, and hand the new value to the user in the session. CONFIRMED 2026-08-16: the seeded login signed in on the live instance on the first try, minutes after the deploy went ready."
  - "⛔ THE PASSWORD-CHANGE ROUTE MOVED. On the current -latest build the rotation endpoint is POST /api/me/password {currentPassword,newPassword}; the older POST /api/users/<id>/password returns 404 — and it is a Next.js HTML not-found page, NOT a JSON error, so it does not read like a routing problem at a [infra]. Hit it 2026-08-16 with the instance already live on the documented default login: the sign-in step succeeded and only the rotate step failed, which is the worst possible half-state. Try /api/me/password FIRST and fall back to the id-based path. Cheap way to find the live route on any build: GET the candidates with the bearer token — the one that exists answers 405 (wrong method), a missing one answers 404."
  - "⛔ SET APP_SECRET EXPLICITLY. It signs the session cookies. Left unset, Umami derives one from the database connection string, so the day anything about that string changes (a rotated database password, a rebuilt managed DB, a move between environments) every existing session is invalidated and every logged-in user is silently signed out. Generate one long random value, pass it as env, and keep passing the SAME one on every redeploy."
  - "DATABASE: Umami reads DATABASE_URL natively, and deploy_compose with database:'managed' APPENDS DATABASE_URL to the project .env already. This is the easy one: unlike n8n there is no remapping to do. Your compose still has to reference it explicitly (DATABASE_URL: \"\${DATABASE_URL}\"), because deploy_compose writes the .env and never edits your compose file. Umami creates its own tables inside whatever database it is given, so the names do not matter — note the DB is named after the DEPLOYMENT, not `app`: deploy #419 with name:'umami' produced database `umami` on VM `db-umami` (pass db_name/db_user to override)."
  - "⛔ DO NOT ADD CLICKHOUSE. The redu MCP has a standing rule that analytics apps which store every event (Plausible, PostHog, Matomo, SigNoz) need a SECOND datastore and tells you to pass needs_clickhouse:true. Umami on the postgresql image does NOT: it stores events in the same Postgres. There is a separate ClickHouse build of Umami, and this is not it. Following the general rule here provisions a whole managed ClickHouse the app never connects to, and quietly doubles the bill."
  - "PORT 3000. The container listens there and the healthcheck Umami ships hits http://localhost:3000/api/heartbeat, which is also the cheapest thing to curl from the VM to prove the app is really up rather than merely running."
  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. Umami runs its own Prisma migrations at container start. On a fresh managed Postgres the first boot takes noticeably longer than later ones while it creates the schema; that is not a hang."
  - "TRACKING SCRIPT: the snippet Umami hands you points at /script.js on the instance's own hostname, so it works on the *.redu.cloud URL with no extra wiring. If the user later moves it to their own domain, the snippet they already pasted into their site keeps pointing at the old host."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.045/hr; fits the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), database:'managed', db_engine:'postgres', db_flavor_id:'2' (m1.small; OMITTING db_flavor_id defaults the DB VM to the app flavor and doubles the bill), port 3000."
  - "PLAN_DEPLOY WILL SIZE THIS AT m1.large — OVERRIDE IT. needs_compose:true raises the app VM to a build-capable floor (m1.large, GBP 0.0486/hr) because it assumes a compose stack builds something. This one builds NOTHING; it pulls a published image. Left alone the plan quotes GBP 0.066/hr against a real GBP 0.0452/hr, so pass flavor_id '3' to deploy_compose explicitly. plan_deploy raises this itself as the `flavor-differs-from-record` preflight once this file records m1.medium — answer it by keeping m1.medium. Measured on m1.medium: pull + first boot + Prisma migrations on an empty DB completed in about 5.5 minutes total, so the small VM is not the bottleneck."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source, so there is no repo to point deploy_compose at. Write a one-service docker-compose.yml locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Passing the Umami GitHub URL would make redu try to build the app instead of pulling the published image."
  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. redu.md is committed and read by the next person. The admin password you set and the APP_SECRET you generate are the user's, not yours to publish. Hand both over in the session and tell them to store them. The deploy log records THAT the account was secured, never what it was secured with."
  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back, adding anything you hit that is not already here. The next person's deploy starts from yours."
  - "DELETING IT LEAVES THE DATABASE BEHIND, ON PURPOSE. delete_deployment removes the app VM but deliberately keeps the managed Postgres so analytics history is not lost by accident, and that DB keeps billing at GBP 0.0174/hr. To stop paying entirely the user must also delete_database."

# Self-host Umami on redu

Privacy-first web analytics you own: one container, a managed Postgres beside it, a public HTTPS
URL. No cookie banner needed, and the visitor data never leaves infrastructure you control.

## What this deploys

- **Umami** from the official prebuilt image, on one m1.medium VM, port 3000.
- **Managed Postgres** on its own private VM, so your analytics history survives every redeploy.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

About GBP 0.045/hour. Inside the no-card free trial. Delete it any time.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## The two that actually break it

**The default login.** Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login value is printed in
Umami's own public documentation. Your instance is on the internet the second it is healthy.
Change it immediately, not later.

**The app secret.** Set `APP_SECRET` yourself and keep it. Without it Umami derives the session
signing key from the database connection string, so the day that string changes, everyone is
logged out.

## Securing the admin account

Do this the moment the deploy reports ready, before you look at anything else. The rotation
endpoint moved between builds, so the script tries `/api/me/password` (current) before the older
`/api/users/<id>/password`; on 2026-08-16 only the first existed, and the second returned an HTML
404 page while the seeded login was already working on the live instance.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Change Umami's seeded admin password, and PROVE the new one works.
#   ./secure-admin.sh umami-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -eu
HOST="${1:?usage: secure-admin.sh <host>}"

TMP=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT

# Alphanumeric only, so there is nothing to escape in JSON or in the shell.
NEW="U7$(LC_ALL=C tr -dc 'A-Za-z0-9' < /dev/urandom | head -c 30)"

# Umami's docs publish the first-login value; read it from the environment rather than
# hardcoding it here, so this file never carries a credential.
CURRENT="${UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD:[REDACTED:value] UMAMI_INITIAL_PASSWORD to the documented first-login value}"

api() { curl -sS -o "$TMP/body" -w '%{http_code}' "$@"; }

# 1. sign in with the seeded account and keep the token.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "login with the seeded account failed: HTTP $code" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }
TOKEN=[REDACTED:value] -n 's/.*"token":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body")
USERID=$(sed -n 's/.*"id":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' "$TMP/body" | head -1)
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] || { echo "signed in but no token came back" >&2; exit 1; }

# 2. rotate it. The route MOVED: current -latest images serve /api/me/password, older ones
#    /api/users/<id>/password. Try both — a build that lacks the route answers with an HTML
#    404 page, not JSON, so a single hardcoded path fails silently-looking on a live instance.
rotated=""
for path in "/api/me/password" "/api/users/$USERID/password"; do
  code=$(printf '{"currentPassword":"%s","newPassword":"%s"}' "$CURRENT" "$NEW" \
    | api -X POST "https://$HOST$path" \
          -H "authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then rotated="$path"; break; fi
  echo "  $path -> HTTP $code" >&2
done
[ -n "$rotated" ] || { echo "password change failed on every known route" >&2; cat "$TMP/body" >&2; exit 1; }

# 3. a 200 does NOT prove the new value works. Sign in again with it; that is the proof.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$NEW" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] || { echo "the change returned 200 but the new value does not sign in: HTTP $code" >&2; exit 1; }

# 4. and prove the old one is dead.
code=$(printf '{"username":"admin","password":"[REDACTED:value]"}' "$CURRENT" \
  | api -X POST "https://$HOST/api/auth/login" -H 'content-type: application/json' --data-binary @-)
[ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "the documented default STILL signs in. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 1; }

cat <<EOF

Admin account secured, and the new sign-in was verified.
  URL:      https://$HOST
  Username: admin
  New:      $NEW

Store this now. A default deploy has no SMTP, so there is no reset by email.
EOF
```

It prints the new value once. It does not go in this file.

## https://umami-7dc25mmx.redu.cloud

**Your credentials — store these now, there's no SMTP so no email reset:**

```
Username:    admin
Password:    «REDACTED:assigned:684aa3e9»
APP_SECRET:  «REDACTED:assigned:f22040b2»
```

The `APP_SECRET` matters on redeploy: pass the **same** value (and the same `dname`) or every logged-in session is invalidated. Neither value is written into redu.md.

**Verified, not assumed:** heartbeat 200 · `/script.js` serves 200 · login with the new password 200 · login with the documented default **401**.

**What's running:** deployment #419, m1.medium app VM + managed Postgres `umami` (db #122) on its own private VM, port 3000, upload-mode compose pulling the prebuilt image. **GBP 0.0452/hr (~GBP 33/mo)**, the planned figure — I overrode plan_deploy's m1.large sizing, which would have been GBP 0.066/hr for a stack that builds nothing. Ready in 5m17s.

**One thing went wrong, and it's the dangerous one.** The rotation script in redu.md posts to `/api/users/<id>/password`, which this image answers with a 404 — but the *login* step succeeded first. One gap: I couldn't confirm `APP_SECRET` inside the container — the SSH command was blocked by the permission classifier. It's wired by construction (passed as `env` → project `.env` → `${APP_SECRET}` in the compose), and a failure here would be silent rather than visible, so tell me if you want me to retry that check with SSH allowed.

# Session report — deploying Umami on redu.cloud

**Date:** 2026-08-16
**Account:** «REDACTED:env:013044ef» (OAuth, verified by `whoami` round-trip)
**Task:** *"Read redu.md and deploy Umami on redu."*
**Outcome:** deployed, secured, verified, documented, then torn down on request.

---

## 1. What was deployed

| | |
|---|---|
| Deployment | `#419`, name `umami`, runtime `compose` |
| URL | `https://umami-7dc25mmx.redu.cloud` (dname pinned up front) |
| App VM | `35e4deae-6542-4438-a59e-654a4e343748` — m1.medium, 2 vCPU / 4 GB / 40 GB |
| Private IP | `[ip]` (floating `[ip]`) |
| Image | `docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami:postgresql-latest` (prebuilt, nothing built from source) |
| Port | 3000 |
| Database | managed Postgres `umami`, db `#122`, VM `db-umami`, m1.small, private-network only |
| Source mode | upload (tarball), **not** git |
| Keypair | `redu-deploy-test` |
| Network | `f7102e8d-9800-48d7-80a9-8369091d7cad` |
| Cost | **GBP 0.0452/hr ≈ GBP 32.99/mo** (app 0.0278 + DB 0.0174) |
| Time to live | **5 min 17 s** from deploy call to first HTTP 200 |

---

## 2. Sequence of work

### 2.1 Read the brief
`redu.md` was read in full. It is an unusually opinionated deploy note: 13 recorded quirks, a
pinned plan (m1.medium / flavor_id `3`, managed Postgres via `db_flavor_id "2"`, port 3000), and
an embedded `secure-admin.sh` for rotating the seeded admin password. Its instructions were
followed as the primary source, with `plan_deploy`'s output treated as advisory.

### 2.2 Preflight
- `whoami` → credential verified, quota 9 instances / 16 vCPU / 34 GB RAM available.
- `check_deploy_prerequisites` → `ready: true`, auto-selected network and keypair.
- `list_flavors` → confirmed `flavor_id "3"` really is m1.medium at 0.0278/hr and `"2"` is
  m1.small at 0.0174/hr, rather than trusting redu.md's mapping unchecked. Passing the wrong id
  here is the difference between GBP 33/mo and GBP 66/mo.

### 2.3 Local artifacts
A one-service `docker-compose.yml` was written (no build stanza, `restart: always`, explicit
`DATABASE_URL` and `APP_SECRET` references, healthcheck on `/api/heartbeat`). `APP_SECRET` was
generated with `openssl rand -hex 32`.

### 2.4 Plan and approval
`plan_deploy` was called with `redu.md` and the compose file pasted verbatim, `needs_postgres:
true`, **`needs_clickhouse: false`**, port 3000.

The plan, the cost, and two deliberate deviations were shown to the user, and **no billed resource
was created until they approved.**

### 2.5 Deploy
`prepare_upload` → tarball 6788 bytes → uploaded; the response's `size_bytes` was checked equal to
the local byte count before the token was used. Then `deploy_compose` with `flavor_id "3"`,
`database: managed`, `db_engine: postgres`, `db_flavor_id "2"`, `db_version 16`, port 3000,
`APP_SECRET` via `env`, and the pre-generated `dname`.

Provisioning was polled to `ready`; a background watcher polled `/api/heartbeat` until it returned
200, which is the real proof the app runs rather than merely that the VM exists.

---

## 3. Judgement calls made against the tooling's defaults

### 3.1 Refused the m1.large sizing — saved ~GBP 15/mo
`plan_deploy` sized the app VM at **m1.large** (GBP 0.066/hr, GBP 48.18/mo) because
`needs_compose: true` raises every compose stack to a build-capable floor. This stack builds
nothing — it pulls a published image — and `redu.md` recorded m1.medium as what actually ran. The
tool itself surfaced the disagreement as a `flavor-differs-from-record` preflight rather than
silently resolving it; it was answered by passing `flavor_id "3"` explicitly.

**Real cost 0.0452/hr against a quoted 0.066/hr.**

### 3.2 Refused to provision ClickHouse
The redu MCP has a standing rule that analytics products (Plausible, PostHog, Matomo, SigNoz)
need a second events datastore, and `plan_deploy` documents under-quoting by a whole tier when
it is omitted. Umami on the **postgresql** image is the exception: it stores events in the same
Postgres. Following the general rule would have provisioned a managed ClickHouse the app never
opens a connection to, roughly doubling the bill.

### 3.3 Set `APP_SECRET` explicitly
Left unset, Umami derives the session-signing key from the database connection string, so a
rotated DB password silently logs out every user. Generated once, passed as env, and recorded as
a value that must be reused on every redeploy.

### 3.4 Pinned the hostname before provisioning
`dname` was generated locally in the exact `<label>-<8 chars>.redu.cloud` form and passed in, so
the URL was known before anything existed and survives redeploys — which matters because Umami's
tracking snippet embeds the instance hostname in customers' sites.

---

## 4. The security incident (the important part)

`redu.md` warns that Umami seeds an `admin` account whose first-login password is printed in
Umami's own public install docs, and that the instance is reachable the moment it is healthy.
The rotation script was staged in advance and run the second the heartbeat returned 200.

**It failed halfway.** The script's step 1 — *sign in with the seeded account* — **succeeded**.
Step 2 — *rotate the password* — returned **HTTP 404**, because `POST /api/users/<id>/password`
does not exist on this build. The 404 arrived as a Next.js **HTML not-found page**, not a JSON
error, so it does not read like a routing problem at a [infra].

That is the worst possible half-state: a live, internet-reachable instance whose publicly
documented login demonstrably works, and a rotation that did not happen.

**Resolution.** Rather than guessing paths, candidate routes were probed with GET using the
bearer token — a route that exists answers **405** (wrong method), a missing one answers **404**:

```
GET /api/me                 -> 200
GET /api/me/password        -> 405   <- exists, POST-only: this is the route
GET /api/users/<id>/password-> 404
GET /api/auth/password      -> 404
GET /api/users/me/password  -> 404
```

The script was amended to try `/api/me/password` first and fall back to the id-based path, then
re-run. It rotated, and — as the script requires — **proved** the result rather than trusting the
200: signed in with the new value (200) *and* confirmed the documented default is dead (401).

Total window in which the instance was live with the documented default: a few minutes, all of it
under active work to close it.

---

## 5. Why the endpoint moved: the registry investigation

`redu.md` advised pinning a version tag "once you know which one you ran". That turned out to be
impossible, and finding out why explained the 404.

Method: `docker.umami.is` 401s on the registry API with
`www-authenticate: realm="https://ghcr.io/token"` — it is a proxy in front of ghcr.io, so an
anonymous pull token from ghcr.io works. With that token, the tag list and each tag's manifest
digest were compared against the digest `postgresql-latest` resolves to.

| Tag | Digest | Image built |
|---|---|---|
| `postgresql-latest` | `sha256:87312d33…` | **2026-08-12** |
| `postgresql-3.0.0` / `-3.0` / `-3` | `sha256:818105b0…` | 2025-11-07 |
| `postgresql-v2.20.2` | `sha256:950133e4…` | 2025-12-12 |
| `postgresql-v2.20.1` | `sha256:73ca19b4…` | — |

**`postgresql-latest` matches no published version tag and is ~8 months newer than the newest
one.** It is a rolling build ahead of the tagged releases — which is exactly why its API surface
had moved on from what redu.md's script expected. The correct pin is therefore the digest:

```
docker.umami.is/umami-software/umami@sha256:«REDACTED:longhex:69c7fc1c»
```

One trap worth recording: digests must be compared with an **identical `Accept` header** across
calls. A different Accept returns a different manifest representation and therefore a different
digest, which looks like a version change when nothing moved. That produced one false mismatch
mid-investigation before headers were normalised.

---

## 6. Verification (measured, not assumed)

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/heartbeat` | **200** |
| `GET /script.js` (tracking script) | **200** |
| `POST /api/auth/login` with the new password | **200** |
| `POST /api/auth/login` with the documented default | **401** (dead) |
| Upload integrity | response `size_bytes` 6788 == local tarball bytes |
| Deployment status | `ready`, phase `done`, healthy=1 on port 3000 |

**Not verified:** that `APP_SECRET` is present *inside* the running container. It is wired by
construction (`env` → project `.env` → `${APP_SECRET}` in the compose), but the confirming SSH
command was blocked by the permission classifier. A failure here would have been silent rather
than visible, so it is recorded as unverified rather than assumed good.

---

## 7. Documentation written back

**`redu.md`** — updated via `get_deployment(redu_md: …)` for a server-side merge (mode:
`in_place`). The merge was diffed before writing: it carried every existing line verbatim and
added only `last_deploy` plus one log line. New and corrected quirks contributed by this run:

1. **Cannot pin by version tag** — `-latest` is a rolling build ahead of all tags; pin the digest,
   and keep `Accept` headers identical when resolving it.
2. **The password-change route moved** — `/api/me/password` on current builds; the old path
   returns an HTML 404; the 405-vs-404 probe finds the live route on any build.
3. **`plan_deploy` over-sizes this to m1.large** — override with `flavor_id "3"`.
4. **The managed DB is named after the deployment** (`umami`), not `app`.
5. **`docker.umami.is` is a ghcr.io proxy** — auth realm noted for anyone querying the registry.
6. The embedded `secure-admin.sh` was rewritten to try both rotation routes.
7. The seeded-login warning was upgraded from a caution to a **confirmed** observation.

The stale "Not yet deployed" placeholder was replaced with the measured entry: flavor, real hourly
rate, 5m17s timing, pinned dname, and the note that the admin account was secured — recording
*that* it was secured, never what with.

**`redu-deploy-plan.md`** — the pre-deploy estimate was replaced with `get_deployment`'s real
provisioned values (live URL, VM id, private IP, real flavor and cost, infra diagram), plus a
combined cost table and redeploy instructions.

**Credentials were never written to any file.** The admin password and `APP_SECRET` were handed
over in the session only, per redu.md's standing rule that the file is committed and read by the
next person.

---

## 8. Teardown

Requested at the end of the session. `delete_deployment` removes the app VM but **deliberately
keeps the managed Postgres** so analytics history is not lost by accident — and that DB keeps
billing at GBP 0.0174/hr until deleted separately.

- **Deployment `#419` (app VM): deleted.**
- **Managed Postgres `#122`: see the note appended below** — a separate, irreversible deletion
  that was raised with the user rather than assumed.

---

## 9. Files left in this directory

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `redu.md` | The living deploy note — now carrying this run's corrections for the next person |
| `redu-deploy-plan.md` | Real provisioned values from the deploy (replaced the estimate) |
| `docker-compose.yml` | The one-service stack that was deployed |
| `session-report-2026-08-16-umami-redu.md` | This report |

content.content: File created successfully at: /home/milos/Desktop/tests_lib/umami/session-report-2026-08-16-umami-redu.md (file state is current in your context — no need to Read it back)
